Why I made this

Music is a big part of my life. I listen pretty much nonstop throughout the day, so I wanted to see what I could do with my own Spotify listening data. I treated this project as a mental jungle gym: a chance to test my capabilities, reshape the data in different ways, and figure out what I could learn from it. The result is a set of experiments looking at the language in song titles, repetition, and how my listening changed over time.

How does repeated listening change the language profile of a music collection? This project turns a Spotify export into an auditable title corpus, then tests how weighting, metadata cleaning and sampling volume change the answer.

NoteResearch frame

This is an independent, exploratory extension inspired by LING 343, not an assignment-specific claim about its syllabus. The evidence is song-title metadata, not lyrics, audio, emotional state or language comprehension.

1 The result in three observations

  1. The counting unit changes the answer. “You” appears in more distinct artist/title pairs than “I” (741 versus 679), but “I” appears in more listening records (3,010 versus 2,765). The ordering also survives the ≥30-second sensitivity filter.
  2. Some apparent vocabulary is release annotation. “Knebworth” and “Wembley” rank highly in full-title salience. A narrow suffix-removal experiment tests how venue and release information contribute, without silently rewriting the primary corpus.
  3. The collection becomes less repetitive near the end of the window. Expected distinct pairs per 500 records rise from 405.3 in December 2025 to 480.9 in October 2026. Effective artist diversity rises from 244.4 to 513.1. These summaries describe this export; they do not identify a cause.

2 Corpus design and privacy

The source archive hash was matched before analysis. Only the six music-history JSON files were read. The analytical input retains month, artist, title and milliseconds played. Account information and exact timestamps are absent. Repeated rows are intentionally retained: after timestamp minimization, identical rows may represent separate plays.

Measure Value
Exported records 55,643
Known artist/title records 53,443
Excluded unknown metadata 2,200
Distinct exact artist/title pairs 12,622
Recorded listening hours 2,575.5

The archive window is 5 November 2025 through 5 November 2026. November at each end is partial, so the central monthly comparison uses December 2025 through October 2026. “Known” excludes records with the literal unknown-artist or unknown-track placeholders. Exact artist/title pairs are proxies for recordings: different recordings can share the same strings, and alternate display names can split a recording.

Data scope: this public report presents aggregate results from my listening history. The original export, account information, exact listening timestamps, and individual listening records are not included.

3 Experiment 1: types, records and denominator choice

A word is counted at most once within a title, even if it repeats. In the first weighting, every distinct artist/title pair contributes once. In the second, each listening record contributes once. These are analogues of type and repeated-token exposure, but the exact observational units are explicit rather than assumed.

word weighting numerator denominator Percent
i Distinct pairs 679 12622 5.379
i Listening records 3010 53443 5.632
you Distinct pairs 741 12622 5.871
you Listening records 2765 53443 5.174
we Distinct pairs 115 12622 0.911
we Listening records 340 53443 0.636
not Distinct pairs 63 12622 0.499
not Listening records 243 53443 0.455
love Distinct pairs 389 12622 3.082
love Listening records 1756 53443 3.286

The ≥30-second check recomputes both denominators: 44,091 records and 11,769 distinct pairs. It is a duration filter, not a skip classifier or proof of active attention. No recording durations or skip flags are available.

Linguistic connection. The pronouns I, you and we invite questions about deixis and person, while not invites questions about negation. The calculation only detects literal forms. It does not resolve speakers or addressees, and not misses contracted negation such as don’t. Love is a word-form probe, not a validated emotion category.

4 Experiment 2: an open vocabulary, with an explicit comparison

For each eligible word, the descriptive score compares its share of records with its share of distinct pairs. An additive constant of 0.5 avoids fragile ratios. The score is

S(w)=log⁡2[(rw+0.5)/(R+1)(pw+0.5)/(P+1)].S(w)=\log_2\left[\frac{(r_w+0.5)/(R+1)}{(p_w+0.5)/(P+1)}\right].

Here, rwr_w and pwp_w are record and pair counts containing the word, and RR and PP are their denominators. A positive score means repeated listening amplifies that word relative to the available title-pair distribution. This is not a statistical significance test. All 279 eligible words are available in the explorer below.

Tokenization lowercases with ICU, extracts Unicode letters and combining marks, preserves accents and splits apostrophes. There is no stemming, lemmatization, language identification or semantic tagging. The open vocabulary keeps tokens of at least two characters, excludes documented stopword and release-word lists, and requires at least 20 distinct pairs. Those modeling choices live in config.R and can be changed deliberately.

5 Experiment 3: annotation is a measurement decision

The sensitivity rule removes only trailing parenthetical or dashed suffixes beginning with live, remaster, remastered or a four-digit year plus remaster(ed). It does not strip every parenthesis or every hyphen. This affects 1,458 pairs and 8,030 records. Original pair IDs and denominators remain fixed so the experiment isolates title-text changes rather than merging recordings.

The chart shows the largest absolute shifts among words passing the threshold in both versions. A word absent from that comparison is not necessarily absent from the corpus. The independent token-count diagnostic below measures actual presence without the salience threshold:

Word Full Suffix_removed
knebworth knebworth 377 0
wembley wembley 494 0
august august 448 26
look look 287 287
away away 690 690
love love 1756 1756

This is a practical corpus-design lesson: display titles mix lexical content with catalog conventions. The narrower rule is a sensitivity experiment, not a claim that every removed token is uninteresting or that the remaining title is linguistically complete.

6 Experiment 4: compare diversity at a common sample size

Raw unique-title counts depend strongly on monthly listening volume. Rarefaction asks how many distinct pairs would be expected in a sample of 500 records drawn without replacement from each month’s empirical records:

E[S500]=∑i[1−(N−ni500)(N500)].E[S_{500}]=\sum_i\left[1-\frac{{N-n_i\choose 500}}{{N\choose 500}}\right].

The implementation uses log combinations and expm1 for numerical stability. It computes the exact expectation; it does not randomly discard data. Months with fewer than 500 records return missing rather than extrapolating.

Artist diversity uses Shannon’s effective number, exp⁡[−∑ipilog⁡(pi)]\exp[-\sum_i p_i\log(p_i)]. This expresses entropy in interpretable units: the number of equally frequent artists with the same diversity. It combines richness and evenness, so it should not be read as the raw artist count.

7 Experiment 5: lexical change and repertoire change

A fixed retrospective vocabulary of 1,273 words is constructed from the full known corpus, using the same explicit exclusions but a minimum of five distinct pairs. Each month assigns a word the number of records whose title contains it, then normalizes these masses across the fixed vocabulary. A multiword title can contribute to several word masses. This distribution is therefore not the same as the word-presence percentages in Experiment 1.

Adjacent monthly distributions are compared using Jensen–Shannon divergence, base 2, with values from 0 to 1. The implementation handles zero masses directly and compares aligned supports. Artist and pair-composition divergences are included as descriptive context.

For September to October, vocabulary divergence is 0.0573, artist-composition divergence 0.2185, and pair-composition divergence 0.5126. The category spaces differ, so their magnitudes are not equivalent scales of “change.” They nevertheless motivate a useful follow-up question: which lexical features remain common as the repertoire turns over? The vocabulary was chosen retrospectively, so this is not a prospective prediction experiment.

9 Reproduce, challenge and extend

Run from the project root:

Rscript --vanilla -e 'source("run_analysis.R"); source("validate_reference.R"); source("publication_plots.R")'
quarto render report.qmd

The core is organized as small functions with validated inputs and explicit configuration. Outputs include the corpus audit, full salience table, monthly distributions, co-occurrence edges with Jaccard overlap, annotation examples, input hash, configuration snapshot and session information. Figures are exported as PNG and vector PDF. Base unit checks cover Unicode tokenization, within-title deduplication, unknown metadata, repeated rows, duration denominators, invalid durations, rarefaction identities, Jensen–Shannon identities and conservative suffix handling. Independent reference assertions check real-data totals and numerical results.

What makes the project advanced: explicit observational units, stable combinatorial computation, aligned probability distributions, modular functions, test fixtures, sensitivity analysis, numerical parity checks and a fully local interactive report. Extra frameworks are not needed to make those choices rigorous.

Useful next experiments: manually annotate a small title sample for person, negation and ambiguity; compare alternate tokenization rules; vary the salience frequency threshold; and examine artist-stratified summaries. If inferential claims are desired, define an estimand and a dependence-aware resampling design first. Repeated records and titles nested within artists are not independent observations.

Limits: one person’s retrospective export; no causal inference, demographic inference or mood classification; no external reference corpus; titles are not lyrics; exact strings are imperfect recording identifiers; genre and language are unvalidated; export completeness cannot be established from these files alone.

10 Sources and method references

  • vegan rarefaction documentation, including the Hurlbert (1971) expected-richness formulation. This implementation computes that expectation without discarding records.
  • SciPy Jensen–Shannon documentation. Its named function returns the square root of divergence (a distance); this report plots divergence itself.
  • Reproducibility details and actually executed checks are recorded in EXECUTION_NOTES.md and outputs/sessionInfo.txt.
